latin.143:
§. XII.
Adhuc Annotationis nostrae primae MEMBRUM PRIMUM expedivimus, ipsius Augustanae Confessionis Naturam concernens; sequitur, ut ad MEMBRUM SECUNDUM delati, de Confessionis ejusdem Theologis & Sociis promiscuè, pro instituti nostri ratione, paucis agamus. Ubi omnium primò distinguendum arbitramur, inter Latè & Strictè sic appellandos.
latin.144: Ad prius genus referimus, quotquot, etiam extra fines Germaniae constituti, vel (1) totam Augustanam Confessionem approbant eique subscribere parati sunt (quales olim fuerunt Bucerus & Calvinus, de quorum priori passim Chytraeus Hist. sua pag. 651. & 656. 659.; de posteriori Auctor der ausführlicher Behauptung 20. peculiari disquisitione: Ob Herr Joh. Calvinus seeliger für einen Augspurgischen Confessions-Verwandten zu seiner Zeit sey gehalten worden/ oder nicht? a pag. 72. ad 90. Adde Pareum in Irenico pag. 293.);
latin.145: Vel (2.) plerisque saltem dictae Confessionis, sincero animo adstipulantur, licèt ob duriorem unam vel alteram Articuli, maximè decimi, phrasin haud omnino admissam, nec amplexi Confessionem in totum sint, nec ei subscripserint, à Subscriptione vel semet abstinentes ipsos, vel ab aliis prohibiti: Quales Tetrapolitani vulgò dicti, Argentinenses, Memmingenses, Constantienses & Lindavienses, Zwinglii Dogma de S. Coena olim secuti, exhibitâ ob id peculiari in Comitiis Augustanis, Confessione, una tamen, cum Augustana, à Caesare rejicienda. Chytr. pag. 678. 679. Renuisse hos subscribere Augustanae Confessioni, ostendunt passim Nostrates, Pareus, Georgius Pauli, &c. aliis interim e Chytraeo Historia, pag. 130. sustinentibus, eos à subscribendo, ex Statuum Protestanticorum sententia, per plura saltem, coercitos fuisse.
latin.146: (3.) Ne illi quidem, latiori hûc sensu, Theologorum Sociorumque Augustanae Confessionis nomine, omnino indigni aestimandi, qui pro locorum temporumque circumstantiis, in hoc, vel isto Regno ac Principatu, August. Confess., utcunque, quà Substantiam, verbo Dei congruam à se habitam, multorum tamen malorum facem, per accidens saltem, futuram veriti, subscriptioni ejusdem semet subduxerunt: Quale quid Theod. Beza & Pet. Martyr, in Colloquio Possiaceno in Gallia fecisse feruntur. Videatur Pareus Iren. pag. 294. 295. Joh. Crocius, Comment in August. Conf. pag. 144. & seqq.
latin.147: Ratio Assertionis nostrae haec est, quòd, ex una parte, qui Confessionem aliquam approbant, illi se eidem associasse animo, intelliguntur; ex altera verò parte, per ipsam Christianae alicujus Confessionis Christianorumque Confitentium Naturam, nemo non hujusmodi Confessioni consentiens, ejusdem socius reputari consuevit.
latin.148: Ad posterius verò genus pertinent, primariò quidem ac immediatè, vel potiùs primò quà ordinem & prioritatem temporis, Imperii Romano-Germanici STATUS OMNES, quorum nomine Confessio August. confecta atque exhibita est, quique eandem manibus suis subscripserunt, unà cum Theologis, Confessionem illam vel adornantibus, vel operam suam quamcunque ad ejus adornationem conferentibus; secundario & mediatè dictorum Imperii Statuum, aliorum quoque, horum exemplum secutorum, Successores universi cum suis Theologis, in hanc usque diem, August. Confess. vel Invariatam solam, vel solam Variatam, vel utramque, ceu re ac Substantia Veritatis unam eandemque, defendentibus, Lutheranorum, sive Reformatorum proprio veniant nomine, communi aliàs Protestantium seu Evangelicorum & γνησίως Catholicorum appellatione, Pontificiis, seu Papam infallibile Universae Ecclesiae caput, summam tàm in Temporalibus, quàm in Spiritualibus tenens potestatem, agnoscentibus, contradistinguendi; sive Articulum Augustanae Confessionis X., de Spirituali & Sacramentali tantum praesentia & exhibitione Corporis & Sanguinis Christi, sive (quod tamen nullibi Augustana Confessio expressit) etiam de Corporali interpretentur:
latin.149: Nam istos non minus, atque hos, August. Confess. Socios habitos semper fuisse (1.) exemplo FRIDERICI PALATINI in Conventu Naumburgico Anno 1561. & Comitiis Augustanis Anno 1566. constat; qua de re prolixius Auctor der ausführlichen Behauptung in Append. a p. 36. ad 43. Pareus in Iren. p. m. 292. & 297. Joh. Crocius in tractatu Germanico nuncupato: Summarische Nachricht und beweißliche Anzeig: Daß die im deutschen Land der Reformirten Religion zugethane Stände und Kirchen/als Mitgenossen der Augspurgischen Confession, des Religions-Friedens fähig seyn/ à num. 123. ad 130. à pag. 54. ad 58. itemque in Comment. de August. Confess. Societate, Questione 2. Cap. XVIII. & Cap. XXI. nec non Dn. D. Becmannus noster l. c. pag. 99. & seqq. (2.) exemplo PHILIPPI, HASSIAE LANDGRAVII, istorum, i.e. Reformatorum partibus constanter faventis, & rigidiores, voce pariter ac scriptis Literis plurimis, in easdem partes, magno cum zelo sollicitantis ac inducentis, apud Chytraeum in Actis cum Zwinglianis, Histor. à pag. 633. & seqq. & apud Calixtum de Tolerantia Reformatorum n. 62. Batavica, & n. 65. novissima Helmst. Edit. nec non in Historia A. C. trium Theologorum germanicè conscripta & a Chemnitii genero in Lat. translata.

pass_a.143: §. XII. Thus far we have dispatched the FIRST MEMBER of our first Annotation, concerning the Nature of the Augsburg Confession itself; it follows that, carried over to the SECOND MEMBER, we treat briefly, according to the plan of our undertaking, of the Theologians and Associates of that same Confession promiscuously. Where first of all we judge a distinction must be made between those so called Loosely and Strictly.
pass_a.144: To the prior genus we refer as many as, even established outside the bounds of Germany, either (1) approve the whole Augsburg Confession and are ready to subscribe to it (such as formerly were Bucer and Calvin; on the former of whom Chytraeus in his History passim pp. 651 and 656, 659; on the latter the Author of the ausführlicher Behauptung 20 in a peculiar disquisition: Whether the late Herr Joh. Calvin was held in his time for an Augsburg Confession kinsman or not? from p. 72 to 90. Add Pareus in the Irenicum p. 293.);
pass_a.145: Or (2.) they sincerely assent at least to most of the said Confession, although on account of a harder phrasing of one or another Article, especially the tenth, not wholly admitted, they have neither embraced the Confession as a whole nor subscribed to it, either themselves abstaining from Subscription, or prohibited by others: Such as the so-called Tetrapolitans — of Strasbourg, Memmingen, Constance, and Lindau — formerly following Zwingli's dogma on the Lord's Supper, and for that reason exhibiting a peculiar Confession at the Augsburg Diet, yet to be rejected by the Emperor together with the Augsburg. Chytraeus pp. 678, 679. That these refused to subscribe the Augsburg Confession our own writers show passim — Pareus, Georg Pauli, etc. — while others meanwhile, from Chytraeus's History p. 130, maintain that they were coerced from subscribing, at least for several reasons, by the judgment of the Protestant Estates.
pass_a.146: (3.) Nor indeed are those, in this wider sense, to be judged wholly unworthy of the name of Theologians and Associates of the Augsburg Confession, who according to the circumstances of places and times, in this or that Kingdom and Principality, fearing that the Augsburg Confession — which they somehow held as congruent with God's word as to Substance — would nevertheless become, at least by accident, a torch of many evils, withdrew themselves from its subscription: Which sort of thing Theodore Beza and Peter Martyr are said to have done in the Colloquy of Poissy in France. See Pareus Iren. pp. 294, 295; Joh. Crocius, Comment on the Augsburg Conf. p. 144 and following.
pass_a.147: The Reason of our Assertion is this: that, on the one part, those who approve some Confession are understood to have associated themselves to it in mind; but on the other part, by the very Nature of any Christian Confession and of Christians confessing, everyone consenting to such a Confession is accustomed to be reputed its associate.
pass_a.148: But to the latter genus pertain, primarily indeed and immediately, or rather first as to order and priority of time, ALL THE ESTATES of the Romano-German Empire, in whose name the Augsburg Confession was framed and exhibited, and who subscribed the same with their own hands, together with the Theologians either adorning that Confession or contributing whatever labor to its adornment; secondarily and mediately of the said Imperial Estates, and of others also who followed their example, all Successors with their Theologians, to this very day, defending the Augsburg Confession — either the Invariata alone, or the Variata alone, or both, as in the thing and Substance of Truth one and the same — whether they come under the proper name of Lutherans or of Reformed, to be contradistinguished by the common appellation elsewhere of Protestants or Evangelicals and genuinely Catholics from the Pontificals, who acknowledge the Pope as infallible head of the Universal Church holding supreme power both in Temporal and in Spiritual things; whether they interpret Article X of the Augsburg Confession of a Spiritual and Sacramental presence and exhibition only of the Body and Blood of Christ, or (which nevertheless the Augsburg Confession nowhere expressed) even of a Corporal one:
pass_a.149: For that those no less than these have always been held Associates of the Augsburg Confession is established (1.) by the example of FREDERICK THE PALATINE in the Naumburg Convention in the Year 1561 and at the Augsburg Diet in the Year 1566; on which matter more fully the Author of the ausführlichen Behauptung in the Appendix from p. 36 to 43; Pareus in the Iren. pp. 292 and 297; Joh. Crocius in the German tract titled Summarische Nachricht und beweißliche Anzeig: That the Estates and Churches in the German land attached to the Reformed Religion, as fellow-members of the Augsburg Confession, are capable of the Religious Peace — from num. 123 to 130, from p. 54 to 58; likewise in the Comment on the Society of the Augsburg Confession, Question 2, Cap. XVIII and Cap. XXI; and also our Dn. D. Becmann l. c. p. 99 and following. (2.) by the example of PHILIP, LANDGRAVE OF HESSE, constantly favoring the parties of those, i.e. of the Reformed, and with great zeal soliciting and inducing the more rigid, by voice alike and by many written Letters, into the same parties — in Chytraeus in the Acts with the Zwinglians, History from p. 633 and following, and in Calixtus On the Tolerance of the Reformed n. 62 Batavian, and n. 65 of the newest Helmstedt Edition; also in the History of the A. C. of three Theologians written in German and translated into Latin by Chemnitz's son-in-law.

143: §. XII. So far we have finished the first member of this first Annotation — the nature of the Augsburg Confession itself.
Next, under the second member, we treat briefly, as our plan requires, of that Confession's theologians and associates in the broad sense.
First we distinguish those so called loosely from those so called strictly.
144: Under the looser class we put all who, even outside Germany, either (1) approve the whole Augsburg Confession and stand ready to subscribe — as Bucer and Calvin once did.

On Bucer see Chytraeus's History at pp. 651, 656, and 659; on Calvin, the Author of the ausführlicher Behauptung 20, in the special inquiry whether the late John Calvin was counted an Augsburg Confession kinsman in his day (pp. 72–90); add Pareus, Irenicum, p. 293.
145: Or (2) they sincerely agree with most of the Confession, yet because of a harder phrasing in one article or another — above all the tenth — they have neither taken the whole Confession nor subscribed, whether by their own abstention or because others barred them.

Such were the so-called Tetrapolitans of Strasbourg, Memmingen, Constance, and Lindau, who once followed Zwingli on the Supper and therefore presented their own Confession at the Augsburg Diet, which the Emperor meant to reject together with the Augsburg.

Chytraeus, pp. 678–679. Our writers (Pareus, Georg Pauli, and others) show that they refused subscription; others, citing Chytraeus's History p. 130, hold that the Protestant Estates' judgment at least partly forced them not to subscribe.
146: (3) Even those who, for local and temporal reasons, withdrew from subscription are not wholly unworthy of the wider name of Augsburg Confession theologians and associates.
They held the Confession congruent with God's word as to substance, yet feared it would become — at least by accident — a torch of many evils in this or that kingdom or principality.
Beza and Peter Martyr are said to have done this at the Colloquy of Poissy in France. See Pareus, Irenicum, pp. 294–295; Crocius on the Augsburg Confession, p. 144ff.
147: Those who approve a confession are understood to have joined themselves to it in mind.
And by the very nature of a Christian confession and of Christians who confess, everyone who consents to it is customarily counted its associate.
148: Under the stricter class fall, primarily and immediately — or rather first in time — all the Estates of the Holy Roman Empire of the German Nation in whose name the Augsburg Confession was framed and exhibited, and who subscribed it with their own hands, together with the theologians who drafted it or helped in any way.

Secondarily and mediately come all successors of those Estates (and of others who followed their example), with their theologians to this day, who defend the Augsburg Confession — the Invariata alone, the Variata alone, or both as one and the same in the substance of truth — whether under the name Lutheran or Reformed.

They are set apart, under the common name of Protestants or Evangelicals and genuinely Catholic, from the papal party that owns the Pope as infallible head of the universal church with supreme temporal and spiritual power.

It does not matter whether they read Article X of a spiritual and sacramental presence and exhibition only of Christ's body and blood, or even of a corporal presence (which the Augsburg Confession nowhere states).
149: That the Reformed no less than the Lutherans have always been held Augsburg Confession associates appears (1) from Frederick the Palatine at Naumburg in 1561 and at the Augsburg Diet in 1566.

See more fully the Author of the ausführlichen Behauptung, Appendix pp. 36–43; Pareus, Irenicum, pp. 292 and 297; Crocius's German Summarische Nachricht… (nos. 123–130; pp. 54–58), and his Comment on Augsburg Confession Society, Q.2, caps. XVIII and XXI; also our Becmann, loc. cit., p. 99ff.

(2) From Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, who steadily favored the Reformed side and with great zeal pressed the more rigid into it by speech and many letters — in Chytraeus's Acts with the Zwinglians from p. 633ff.; Calixtus, On Tolerance of the Reformed, n. 62 (Batavian) and n. 65 (newest Helmstedt); and the History of the A.C. by three theologians, written in German and Latinized by Chemnitz's son-in-law.
